blocks.content: This is one of the most common DevOps interview questions, and the honest answer is that VMs and containers solve the isolation problem at two different layers of the stack.
1. How a Virtual Machine Achieves Isolation
blocks.text: 1. How a Virtual Machine Achieves Isolation

blocks.content: A hypervisor sits on top of the physical server and carves it into multiple virtual machines. Each virtual machine gets its own complete guest operating system, kernel and all, even if every VM on that host is running the same Linux distribution. The application runs on top of that guest OS.

blocks.alt: Every VM carries its own full operating system

blocks.content: A container does not boot its own kernel. Instead, a container engine (Docker's dockerd) uses features already built into the host's Linux kernel, namely namespaces and cgroups, to give each container the illusion of its own isolated filesystem, process tree, and network stack, while every container on that host is actually sharing one kernel underneath.

blocks.alt: Every container shares the same host kernel

blocks.content: That one architectural difference (a full guest OS per VM versus one shared kernel for all containers) is the source of every other difference you will hear about between VMs and containers.

blocks.alt: Skipping OS boot is the whole reason containers start fast
A VM image carries an entire OS, a container image does not
VMs isolate at the kernel boundary, containers isolate within one kernel

4. When to Actually Reach for Each One
blocks.text: 4. When to Actually Reach for Each One

blocks.content: This is not a "containers are strictly better" story. If you genuinely need to run a different kernel (a Windows workload on Linux hardware, or you need the hardest possible isolation boundary for untrusted, multi-tenant code), a VM is still the right tool. For the overwhelming majority of "package and run my application" use cases, a container is faster, lighter, and simpler to operate.

blocks.alt: The one question that decides it

blocks.content: In practice, most production systems today use both, together: cloud instances are themselves virtual machines, and Docker containers then run inside those VMs, combining the strong tenant isolation of virtualization with the speed and density of containers.

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: A VM virtualizes hardware and boots its own kernel, a container virtualizes the operating system and shares the host's kernel via namespaces and cgroups.
That single architectural difference is why containers start in about a second while VMs take much longer, and why containers pack far more densely onto the same hardware.
In real infrastructure, VMs and containers are not rivals, cloud VMs are usually the hosts that Docker containers run inside of.
